WASHINGTON (CNN) -- As President Obama approaches day 100 of his administration, some in Washington caution that the torture tug-of-war could be a costly distraction. Leg restraints await detainees at Guantanamo Bay in this 2006 photo. Earlier this month, the Obama administration released four Bush-era memos detailing "enhanced interrogations" of suspected al Qaeda members. Now, the White House is reviewing former Vice President Dick Cheney's request to make more memos public. Two weeks before Obama released any memos, Cheney submitted a request to the National Archives calling for the release of other documents. He says that what he requested will prove that the Bush interrogation tactics -- which critics have called a torture program -- worked. "I haven't talked about it, but I know specifically of reports that I read, that I saw, that lay out what we learned through the interrogation process and what the consequences were for the country," Cheney said in an interview with Fox News last week. The White House is signaling that not only is it considering honoring Cheney's request, it may go even further. "I think the president, as you know, is a big believer in transparency," White House press secretary Robert Gibbs said Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press." "I think one of the things that will have to be examined is whether there are additional memos that have to be released that give a broader picture of what's gone on in enhanced interrogation techniques." The almost daily revelations are dividing Democrats between those calling for full disclosure and those urging caution. "We don't just turn the page without reading it. We want to make sure what the mistakes were so that the Obama administration doesn't make these mistakes," Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont. said Sunday. But Sen. Dianne Feinstein, D-California, warned Sunday against moving to quickly. "We need to find these things out, and we need to do it in a way that's calm and deliberative and professional, because I think all of this, on the front burner, before the public, does harm our intelligence gathering, it does harm America's position in the world," she said on CNN's "State of the Union." Across the aisle, Republicans are insisting the Justice Department drop any investigation of Bush administration officials who authorized harsh interrogations. "I think that would be a stab in the back. I think he has already demoralized the CIA, put them in a CYA mode," Sen. Kit Bond, R-Missouri, said Sunday on Fox News. Arizona Sen. John McCain, the former Republican presidential candidate, said prosecuting those who gave legal advice is wrong. "I don't think those memos should have been released, but the fundamental point now is whether to prosecute people who gave the president, in my view, legitimate advice, even though it was wrong," he said.  "We should not be prosecuting people who gave legal advice. It's wrong to do that to them, and it sets a terrible precedent for the future." Rep. Pete Hoekstra of Michigan, the top Republican on the House Intelligence Committee, and House Minority Leader John Boehner of Ohio are calling on the White House to release a list of who was briefed about the interrogation programs. "Congress and the American people deserve a full and complete set of facts about what information was yielded by CIA's interrogation program, and they deserve to know which of their representatives in Congress were briefed about these techniques and the extent of those briefings," Boehner said in a statement Monday. "To date, the administration has fallen short in providing this information. ... The American people have been provided an incomplete picture of exactly what intelligence was made available by the interrogation program," he said. But Connecticut Sen. Joe Lieberman, a Democrat-turned-independent, said the whole debate over the memos is "moot." "What do we gain, first, by releasing the memos; but, secondly, what do we gain from indicting lawyers for their opinions, if that is a possibility here? ... It will poison the water here in Washington. It will achieve nothing. It will make it harder for President Obama to do some of the big things he wants to do for the country," he said.

Two weeks before Obama released any documents, Cheney had submitted a request to the National Archives seeking the release of other materials, asserting that they would demonstrate the effectiveness of the Bush administration's interrogation tactics—methods that critics have characterized as torture.

"I think the president, as you know, is a strong believer in transparency," White House press secretary Robert Gibbs said Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press." "I think one of the things that will have to be examined is whether there are additional memos that need to be released to give a fuller picture of what has transpired regarding enhanced interrogation techniques."

The near-daily stream of revelations is creating a divide among Democrats—between those advocating full disclosure and those urging a more measured approach. "We don't just turn the page without reading it. We want to make sure we understand what the mistakes were, so that the Obama administration doesn't repeat them," Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont, said Sunday.

Sen. Dianne Feinstein, D-California, however, cautioned against moving too quickly. "We need to find these things out, and we need to do it in a way that's calm, deliberative, and professional, because I believe that keeping all of this at the forefront of public attention does harm to our intelligence-gathering efforts and to America's standing in the world," she said on CNN's "State of the Union."

Across the aisle, Republicans are urging the Justice Department to abandon any investigation into Bush administration officials who authorized the harsh interrogation methods. "I think that would be a stab in the back. I believe he has already demoralized the CIA and put it in a defensive posture," Sen. Kit Bond, R-Missouri, said Sunday on Fox News.

Arizona Sen. John McCain, the former Republican presidential candidate, argued that prosecuting those who provided legal counsel would be misguided. "I don't think those memos should have been released, but the fundamental question now is whether to prosecute individuals who gave the president what I consider legitimate advice, even if it was ultimately mistaken," he said. "We should not be prosecuting people for offering legal advice. It would be wrong to do so, and it would set a troubling precedent for the future."

Rep. Pete Hoekstra of Michigan, the ranking Republican on the House Intelligence Committee, and House Minority Leader John Boehner of Ohio have called on the White House to release a full list of those who were briefed on the interrogation programs. "Congress and the American people deserve a complete and accurate account of what information was gained through the CIA's interrogation program, and they deserve to know which members of Congress were briefed on these techniques and the extent of those briefings," Boehner said in a statement Monday. "To date, the administration has fallen short in providing this information. ... The American people have been given an incomplete picture of exactly what intelligence resulted from the interrogation program."

Connecticut Sen. Joe Lieberman, a Democrat-turned-independent, contended that the entire debate over the memos is, in his view, "moot." "What do we gain, first, by releasing the memos; and second, what do we gain by indicting lawyers for their legal opinions, if that is even a possibility here? ... # Interrogation Memo Controversy Threatens to Overshadow Obama's Agenda

As President Obama nears his administration's 100-day milestone, political observers in the capital warn that the ongoing dispute over interrogation techniques could become a significant drain on time and resources.

Recently, the administration disclosed four documents from the Bush era that outlined so-called "enhanced interrogation" methods used on suspected al Qaeda operatives. This action has now prompted White House officials to consider a separate demand from former Vice President Dick Cheney, who wants additional records made public.

Before Obama's release of the initial memos, Cheney had already petitioned the National Archives for supplementary documents. His argument centers on the belief that these materials would demonstrate the effectiveness of interrogation methods that opponents characterize as torture. Speaking with Fox News last week, Cheney stated: "I haven't talked about it, but I know specifically of reports that I read, that I saw, that lay out what we learned through the interrogation process and what the consequences were for the country."

Indications from the White House suggest they're not just contemplating Cheney's request—they might expand the scope of disclosure even further. Press Secretary Robert Gibbs, appearing Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press," noted: "I think the president, as you know, is a big believer in transparency. I think one of the things that will have to be examined is whether there are additional memos that have to be released that give a broader picture of what's gone on in enhanced interrogation techniques."

## Democrats Split on Approach

The steady stream of new information is creating friction among Democrats, with some pushing for complete transparency while others advocate for a more measured approach.

Vermont Senator Patrick Leahy argued Sunday for thorough examination: "We don't just turn the page without reading it. We want to make sure what the mistakes were so that the Obama administration doesn't make these mistakes."

Conversely, California Senator Dianne Feinstein cautioned against rushing forward, telling CNN's "State of the Union": "We need to find these things out, and we need to do it in a way that's calm and deliberative and professional, because I think all of this, on the front burner, before the public, does harm our intelligence gathering, it does harm America's position in the world."

## Republican Pushback

On the other side of the political spectrum, GOP lawmakers are pressing the Justice Department to abandon any investigation into Bush administration officials who approved the harsh interrogation tactics.

Missouri Senator Kit Bond didn't mince words on Fox News: "I think that would be a stab in the back. I think he has already demoralized the CIA, put them in a CYA mode."

Former presidential candidate John McCain of Arizona expressed concern about prosecuting legal advisers: "I don't think those memos should have been released, but the fundamental point now is whether to prosecute people who gave the president, in my view, legitimate advice, even though it was wrong. We should not be prosecuting people who gave legal advice. It's wrong to do that to them, and it sets a terrible precedent for the future."

Meanwhile, House Minority Leader John Boehner and Representative Pete Hoekstra of Michigan, the ranking Republican on the House Intelligence Committee, are demanding the administration disclose which lawmakers received briefings on the interrogation programs. In a Monday statement, Boehner declared: "Congress and the American people deserve a full and complete set of facts about what information was yielded by CIA's interrogation program, and they deserve to know which of their representatives in Congress were briefed about these techniques and the extent of those briefings. To date, the administration has fallen short in providing this information... The American people have been provided an incomplete picture of exactly what intelligence was made available by the interrogation program."

## A Voice for Moving On

Independent Senator Joe Lieberman of Connecticut, who left the Democratic Party, dismissed the entire controversy as pointless. He questioned: "What do we gain, first, by releasing the memos; but, secondly, what do we gain from indicting lawyers for their opinions, if that is a possibility here?... It will poison the water here in Washington. It will achieve nothing. It will make it harder for President Obama to do some of the big things he wants to do for the country."

# The Torture Memo Controversy: A Growing Challenge for the Obama Administration

As President Obama's administration approaches the symbolically significant 100-day mark in office, it finds itself embroiled in an increasingly contentious debate over the release of Bush-era torture memos—a controversy that some political observers warn could evolve into a costly and damaging distraction from the administration's broader policy agenda.

The issue gained further complexity when former Vice President Dick Cheney publicly called on the National Archives to declassify and release additional documents related to the interrogation program. Cheney has argued that these withheld materials would substantiate his long-standing claim that the enhanced interrogation techniques employed during the Bush administration's tenure were not only justified but effective in extracting valuable intelligence and preventing potential terrorist attacks. His request has effectively challenged the current administration to either validate or refute these assertions through the release of additional evidence.

In response to mounting pressure from multiple directions, the White House has signaled a willingness to accommodate Cheney's demand. Press Secretary Robert Gibbs indicated that the administration may indeed honor the request for further disclosure, suggesting that additional memos could be released in the interest of maintaining transparency—a core value the Obama administration has sought to project since taking office. This stance, however, places the White House in a delicate position, balancing its commitment to openness against concerns about national security implications and the potential political fallout from further revelations.

The controversy has also exposed notable divisions within the Democratic Party regarding the appropriate path forward. Senator Patrick Leahy of Vermont has emerged as a vocal proponent of comprehensive disclosure, arguing that a thorough and honest reckoning with the past is essential for the nation to learn from previous mistakes and prevent similar policies from being enacted in the future. Leahy's position reflects a broader sentiment among some Democrats who view full transparency as both a moral imperative and a necessary step toward accountability.

Conversely, Senator Dianne Feinstein of California, who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, has urged a markedly different approach. Feinstein has called for calm, measured, and professional handling of the matter, cautioning against what she perceives as a rush toward disclosure that could compromise ongoing investigations or inadvertently politicize sensitive national security matters. Her stance underscores the tension between those eager to expose past wrongdoing and those wary of the potential consequences of moving too quickly or too publicly.

This split within Democratic ranks illustrates the broader challenge facing the Obama administration: navigating a politically fraught issue that touches on national security, executive accountability, and the party's own internal disagreements—all while attempting to maintain focus on its initial legislative and policy priorities during a critical early period in office.

# Obama Administration Weighs Release of Additional Interrogation Memos Amid Democratic Divide

The Obama administration is currently deliberating whether to release additional Bush-era memos detailing the use of "enhanced interrogation" techniques on terrorism suspects, a decision that has taken on new urgency following a direct challenge from former Vice President Dick Cheney. In recent public statements, Cheney has called on the administration to declassify documents that he asserts will demonstrate the effectiveness of these controversial interrogation methods, arguing that the techniques—which included tactics widely condemned as torture, such as waterboarding—yielded critical intelligence that helped thwart terrorist plots and protect American lives.

Cheney's request has placed the White House in a difficult position, forcing officials to weigh the competing demands of transparency, national security, and political fallout. The administration had already released a set of memos earlier this year outlining the legal justifications used by the Bush administration to authorize these interrogation practices, a move that reignited fierce debate over the ethics and legality of the "war on terror" policies. Now, with Cheney publicly pushing for further disclosure—specifically documents he claims will validate the intelligence value of these methods—the pressure has intensified for the administration to make a decision one way or the other.

This development has exposed a growing and increasingly public rift within the Democratic Party over how to handle the legacy of Bush-era counterterrorism policies. On one side, a faction of Democrats, including some lawmakers and human rights advocates, are pushing hard for complete transparency. They argue that releasing all relevant documents—regardless of political consequences—is essential for the country to fully reckon with past mistakes, hold those responsible accountable, and ensure that such practices are never repeated. For this group, transparency is not just a matter of principle but a necessary step toward institutional accountability and healing.

On the other side, more cautious Democrats, including some senior officials within the administration itself, are urging restraint. They worry that a rapid or piecemeal release of sensitive documents could inadvertently play into Cheney's hands, giving him and other defenders of the Bush-era policies a platform to reframe the debate around effectiveness rather than legality or morality. This camp advocates for a slower, more deliberate approach, one that carefully considers the timing, context, and potential political ramifications of releasing additional information. They fear that mishandling the issue could turn what should be a sober reckoning with past policy into a politically charged spectacle that overshadows the broader goals of accountability and reform.

The debate underscores the delicate balancing act facing President Obama as he navigates the competing pressures of honoring his campaign promises of transparency and accountability while also managing the political risks of reopening old wounds from the Bush era. As the administration continues to weigh its options, the outcome of this decision could have lasting implications—not only for how the country confronts its recent history of counterterrorism policy, but also for the internal cohesion of the Democratic Party as it grapples with how best to move forward.

# White House Grapples With Fallout Over Release of Bush-Era Interrogation Memos

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — The Obama administration is facing intense political crosscurrents this week after the release of Justice Department memos detailing harsh interrogation techniques authorized during the Bush administration, with reactions splitting sharply along partisan lines and even prompting divisions within the president's own coalition.

The memos, written by the Office of Legal Counsel between 2002 and 2005, provided legal justification for techniques including waterboarding, sleep deprivation, and confinement in small boxes, methods used against terrorism suspects including alleged September 11 plotter Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

President Obama, in releasing the documents, said he did so "with reluctance" but felt bound by transparency commitments and pending Freedom of Information Act litigation. He simultaneously moved to shield CIA officers who relied on the legal guidance from prosecution, a decision that has satisfied almost no one entirely.

**Cheney: Release Endangers Americans**

Former Vice President Dick Cheney was among the most vocal critics, arguing the release was reckless and demanding the administration also declassify memos he says demonstrate the interrogation program's effectiveness in preventing attacks.

"They put out the legal memos … but they didn't put out the memos that show the success of the effort," Cheney said in a television interview. "I know specifically of reports that I read, that I saw, that lay out what we learned through the interrogation process and the валue of that information."

Cheney has requested those documents be declassified through official channels, setting up a further confrontation with the administration.

**Leahy Wants a Fuller Accounting**

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy, a Vermont Democrat, said the memos underscored his long-standing call for an independent "truth commission" to examine detainee treatment policies comprehensively.

"The American people deserve a full and fair accounting of what was done in our name," Leahy said, adding that the memos alone don't answer questions about who ordered the techniques and why.

**Feinstein Cites Ongoing Intelligence Committee Review**

Senate Intelligence Committee Chairwoman Dianne Feinstein noted her panel was already conducting its own classified review of CIA detention and interrogation programs, a process she said would produce a more complete picture "based on records rather than public relations."

Feinstein has been notably cautious about calls for prosecutions, urging patience until the committee's review is finished.

**McCain: A Painful but Necessary Reckoning**

Senator John McCain, who was tortured as a prisoner of war in Vietnam and has long opposed such interrogation techniques on moral and practical grounds, offered a more measured response than many of his Republican colleagues.

"I know from personal experience that the abuse of prisoners will produce more bad than good intelligence," McCain said. "I understand and to a large extent agree with the sentiment that we should not be prosecuting people who were operating in good faith based on the legal guidance they were given. But this is a stain that has to be dealt with honestly."

**Boehner Warns of Distraction, Danger**

House Minority Leader John Boehner accused the administration of playing politics with national security and warned that releasing the memos while shielding actual policymakers from scrutiny sent a confused message.

"This is going to have a chilling effect on our intelligence community's willingness to do what's necessary to protect Americans," Boehner said, arguing the White House should instead focus on "growing our economy and keeping Americans safe," rather than "relitigating the past."

**A White House Balancing Act**

White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs reiterated that the administration has "no interest in prosecuting" CIA personnel who acted on legal advice at the time, but declined to rule out further action against those who crafted the legal reasoning itself — leaving open a politically fraught question that is likely to dominate Washington in the weeks ahead.

Attorney General Eric Holder is expected to face pointed questioning on the matter at an upcoming congressional hearing, as lawmakers on both sides continue to press for either broader investigations or an end to what critics call a damaging and divisive reexamination of the past.

*CNN's coverage of this story is ongoing.*

*WASHINGTON* — As President Obama approaches the symbolic 100-day marker of his presidency, a growing controversy over the release of Bush-era interrogation memos threatens to consume the political oxygen that had largely fueled his economic recovery efforts, according to lawmakers and analysts on both sides of the aisle.

The release of previously classified Justice Department memos detailing harsh interrogation techniques authorized during the Bush administration—including waterboarding and other methods widely characterized as torture—has ignited fierce debate in Washington over whether officials involved should face investigation or prosecution.

Republican lawmakers argue the controversy is diverting attention from more pressing matters. "The president has a full plate—the economy, health care, two wars," said one senior GOP member of the House Judiciary Committee, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss internal party strategy. "Relitigating the last administration's legal decisions doesn't create a single job. This is exactly the kind of distraction the country doesn't need right now."

Others in the party have been more pointed. "This administration campaigned on looking forward, not backward," said Rep. Lamar Smith of Texas, ranking Republican on the Judiciary Committee. "Opening the door to prosecutions of intelligence officials sends a chilling message and drags us into a partisan battle at a time when we should be focused on economic recovery."

Democratic lawmakers, however, largely reject the framing that accountability efforts constitute a "distraction."

"We can walk and chew gum at the same time," said Rep. Jerrold Nadler of New York, a member of the Judiciary Committee who has pushed for a full accounting of interrogation practices. "The rule of law isn't a sideshow. If crimes were committed, we have an obligation to address that, regardless of the political calendar."

Senate Judiciary Chairman Patrick Leahy has floated the idea of a "truth commission" to examine the interrogation program, a proposal that has drawn support from human rights advocates but skepticism from centrists in both parties wary of a prolonged, divisive process.

The White House itself has sent mixed signals. President Obama initially indicated CIA operatives who followed legal guidance at the time would not be prosecuted, while leaving the door open regarding those who crafted the legal justifications. That ambiguity has done little to quiet the storm, with commentators on cable news devoting hours to the debate that might otherwise focus on unemployment figures, the administration's housing initiatives, or health care reform groundwork.

Political strategists note the irony: an administration that entered office promising a laser focus on the economy now finds itself fielding daily questions about a legal and moral reckoning over the previous administration's national security policies.

"Every news cycle spent on this is a news cycle not spent explaining the stimulus package or laying groundwork for health care reform," said one Democratic strategist not affiliated with the White House. "That's the real risk here—not that the debate is illegitimate, but that it competes with everything else."

As the 100-day marker approaches, with its inevitable retrospectives and grading of the administration's early performance, the torture memo controversy appears likely to feature prominently in that assessment—for better or worse.

Former Vice President Dick Cheney has renewed his call for the declassification of additional documents related to the CIA's interrogation program, arguing that the records would demonstrate the effectiveness of techniques used on terrorism suspects during the Bush administration. The request has reignited a contentious debate over transparency, national security, and the legacy of post-9/11 counterterrorism policies.

Cheney has repeatedly asserted that the memos in question—reportedly detailing intelligence gathered through the CIA's now-defunct interrogation program—would validate the necessity and success of methods that critics have condemned as torture. He has framed his push as a matter of setting the historical record straight, suggesting that selective disclosure by the Obama administration has painted an incomplete and misleading picture of the program's outcomes.

The White House, however, has offered a measured response. Press Secretary Robert Gibbs addressed the matter during a briefing, indicating that the administration was reviewing Cheney's request but stopped short of committing to swift action. Gibbs emphasized that any declassification decisions would go through appropriate channels, weighing national security considerations against calls for transparency.

Gibbs' comments reflect the administration's broader struggle to balance competing pressures: civil liberties advocates and international critics who have called for full accountability regarding interrogation practices, and defenders of the previous administration who argue that releasing only partial information unfairly maligns officials who crafted counterterrorism policy in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks.

The dispute underscores a deeper tension between the current administration and its predecessor over how the "war on terror" should be remembered. Cheney, who has emerged as one of the most vocal defenders of Bush-era policies since leaving office, has used public appearances and interviews to argue that enhanced interrogation techniques yielded critical intelligence that prevented attacks—a claim that intelligence officials and lawmakers have disputed with varying degrees of certainty.

Gibbs' cautious tone suggests the White House is wary of appearing to either validate or dismiss Cheney's claims outright, mindful that any documents released could reignite legal and political controversies surrounding the treatment of detainees at Guantanamo Bay and other facilities.

As the debate continues, both sides appear entrenched: Cheney pressing for what he considers vindication through additional transparency, and the administration proceeding cautiously, wary of the legal, diplomatic, and political ramifications of further declassification.

# Bush-Era Interrogation Memos Reignite Partisan Battle Over Prosecution

**WASHINGTON** — The release of Justice Department memos detailing harsh interrogation techniques authorized during the Bush administration has opened a new front in Washington's ongoing battle over how to handle the legacy of the CIA's detention program, with lawmakers splitting sharply along party lines over whether officials who crafted the policies should face legal consequences.

The memos, released last week by the Obama administration, provide explicit details about techniques including waterboarding, sleep deprivation, and confinement in small boxes with insects—methods that were authorized for use against terrorism suspects following the September 11 attacks.

## Democrats Push for Accountability

Many Democrats have called the techniques described in the memos tantamount to torture and argued that those who authorized them, from Bush administration lawyers to senior officials, should be investigated.

"When you read these memos, it's hard not to be shocked at the level of detail and the coldness of the analysis," said one senior Democratic lawmaker, who has pushed for a bipartisan commission to investigate the program. "We owe it to the country to understand exactly what was done in our name."

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and other Democratic leaders have faced pressure from their party's base to pursue prosecutions, with some members suggesting a special prosecutor should examine whether Bush administration officials broke domestic and international laws against torture.

Senator Patrick Leahy, chairman of the Judiciary Committee, has continued to advocate for a "truth commission" that would grant immunity to witnesses in exchange for testimony, modeled partly on South Africa's post-apartheid reconciliation process.

## Republicans Warn of Political Retribution

Republicans have largely condemned the release of the memos, arguing it provides a roadmap to America's enemies while doing nothing to enhance national security. Many have characterized talk of prosecutions as a dangerous politicization of intelligence gathering.

"This is nothing more than criminalizing policy differences," said a senior Republican member of the Senate Intelligence Committee. "These lawyers and officials were operating in good faith, trying to protect this country after the worst attack on American soil in our history."

Former Vice President Dick Cheney has been particularly vocal, requesting the declassification of additional memos he says would prove the interrogation program produced valuable intelligence that prevented terrorist attacks. He has criticized the release of the legal memos without the accompanying intelligence assessments as "half the picture."

House Minority Leader John Boehner echoed concerns that the disclosures would harm relationships with intelligence services and complicate future counterterrorism efforts. "Our men and women in the intelligence community now have to wonder if aggressive but lawful actions taken today will be second-guessed and prosecuted tomorrow," he said.

## White House Treads Carefully

President Obama has attempted to navigate a middle path, stating that CIA officers who acted in good faith based on legal guidance at the time would not face prosecution. However, he has notably left open the possibility that those who crafted the legal justifications—including former Justice Department attorneys—could still face scrutiny.

"This is a time for reflection, not retribution," Obama said, though he added that the Attorney General would make determinations about the legal memo authors independent of political considerations.

The administration's position has satisfied neither side fully. Civil liberties groups have criticized the immunity granted to CIA interrogators, while Republicans remain wary that the door has been left open to prosecuting Bush-era lawyers, including former Office of Legal Counsel attorneys John Yoo and Jay Bybee.

## A Divided Path Forward

With Attorney General Eric Holder reportedly reviewing whether to pursue investigations, both parties are bracing for a protracted fight. Democrats controlling Congress face internal divisions of their own, as some worry that pursuing prosecutions could consume the administration's early agenda and invite accusations of partisan vendetta, while others argue that failing to act would represent a failure of oversight and accountability.

Republicans, meanwhile, have begun coordinating messaging warning that any prosecutions would be seen as criminalizing policy disagreements and could deter future officials from making difficult decisions during national security crises.

The debate shows no signs of resolution soon, with both parties dug into positions that reflect broader disagreements about executive power, national security, and how democracies should reckon with controversial decisions made during times of perceived crisis.

---

*This article reflects reporting from April 2009, during the period when the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel memos were declassified and released to the public.*

# Senators Clash Over Interrogation Memos on Sunday Talk Shows

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — The release of Bush-era memos detailing harsh interrogation techniques dominated the Sunday talk show circuit this week, with lawmakers sharply divided over whether officials who authorized the practices should face investigation or prosecution.

Appearing on multiple networks, senior senators offered starkly different assessments of the controversy, which has reignited debate over the boundaries of executive power in the fight against terrorism.

## Calls for Accountability

Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-California), chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said her panel would conduct a "thorough and dispassionate" review of the interrogation program, but stopped short of endorsing a criminal investigation.

"We need to know what was done, in whose name, and whether it made us safer," Feinstein said. "That's different from a prosecution."

Sen. Patrick Leahy (D-Vermont), who has pushed for a "truth commission" style inquiry, reiterated his call for a nonpartisan panel to examine the program, arguing that accountability was essential regardless of political fallout.

"We cannot simply turn the page," Leahy said. "If we don't understand what happened, we can't ensure it never happens again."

## Warnings Against "Criminalizing Policy Differences"

Republican senators pushed back forcefully, warning that pursuing legal action against Bush administration lawyers or CIA officials would set a dangerous precedent.

Sen. John McCain (R-Arizona), a former prisoner of war who has long opposed torture, offered a nuanced position. While reaffirming his belief that waterboarding constituted torture, McCain cautioned against prosecuting those who acted on legal guidance provided at the time.

"I do not believe that we can continue to explore whether there was a violation of the law," McCain said. "I think it's time to move forward."

Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky), the Senate Minority Leader, was more blunt, accusing the administration of playing politics with national security.

"This is about relitigating the past for political purposes," McConnell said. "It will chill future intelligence officers from taking necessary actions to protect the country."

## Administration Officials Signal Caution

White House officials, appearing on the same programs, sought to walk a careful line. Senior adviser David Axelrod said President Obama believed "no one is above the law," but emphasized the administration's focus remained on policy going forward rather than past prosecutions.

"The president has been clear he wants to look forward, not backward," Axelrod said, though he added that any decision on prosecutions would ultimately rest with Attorney General Eric Holder and the Justice Department.

Holder himself, in a separate interview, left the door open to potential legal action against those who exceeded the legal guidance outlined in the memos, though he declined to elaborate further.

## CIA Morale Concerns

Rep. Peter Hoekstra (R-Michigan), ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, expressed concern that the release of the memos — and the ongoing debate over prosecutions — could damage morale within the intelligence community.

"Our intelligence professionals need to know that if they act in good faith, based on legal guidance from the Justice Department, they will not be hung out to dry years later," Hoekstra said.

## What's Next

The debate is expected to intensify this week as Congress returns to Washington, with several committees signaling interest in holding hearings on the matter. Feinstein said her committee's review would take months to complete, while the Justice Department continues its own internal assessment of the legal memos.

The controversy underscores the broader tension facing the Obama administration as it seeks to address the legacy of Bush-era counterterrorism policies while avoiding what officials fear could become a politically polarizing and lengthy legal battle.

*CNN's coverage of this developing story will continue.*
